title: How to build savings for starting a small business in the US
description: Calculating your 'Runway' and separating personal finances from startup capital.
content:
Starting a business is the American Dream, but running out of cash is the nightmare. The #1 reason small businesses fail is under-capitalization. Founders often underestimate the 'Burn Rate'—the cash required to keep the business (and themselves) alive before revenue hits. You cannot rely on business loans for everything; banks rarely lend to new entities without revenue. You need a personal war chest. This guide explains how to save the 'Seed Capital' required to make the leap safely.

Key Takeaways

  • The Two Buckets: You need two savings funds: Personal Survival (Rent/Food) and Business Operations (Inventory/Software). Do not mix them.
  • The Runway Calculation: Calculate how many months you can survive with $0 revenue. 6 months is risky; 12 months is standard.
  • Keep the Day Job: The best investor in your business is your current employer. Build the side hustle using your salary to fund it ('Bootstrapping') until it replaces your income.
  • Liquidity: Keep business savings in a liquid High-Yield Savings Account. Do not put seed money in the stock market.

Why It Matters (US Context)

The SBA (Small Business Administration) defines a 'Microloan' as under $50k. Getting approved is hard. Personal savings account for 60-70% of all startup funding in the US. You are your own Angel Investor.

Calculating the Number

Before you quit, do the math.

Bucket A: Personal Runway

How much do you need to live?

  • Monthly Expenses: $4,000.
  • Health Insurance (COBRA/ACA): +$500.
  • Target: 12 months x $4,500 = $54,000.

Bucket B: Business Seed

What are the startup costs?

  • LLC Formation/Legal: $1,000.
  • Equipment/Laptop: $2,000.
  • Software/Hosting: $500/mo.
  • Inventory/Ads: $5,000.
  • Target: $10,000.

Total Goal: $64,000. Do not quit until this number is in the bank.

How to Fill the Buckets

  1. The 'Double Life': Live on 50% of your salary. Save the rest. It sucks for 2 years, but it buys you freedom.
  2. Separate Accounts: Open a separate HYSA named 'Business Launch'. Do not keep this money in your checking. It is sacred.
  3. Sell Assets: Sell the second car. Downsize the apartment. Liquidity is more important than comfort right now.
  4. Pause Investing: Controversial, but effective. Pause your taxable brokerage contributions. Divert that cash flow to the Business Fund. Investing in yourself potentially has a higher ROI than the S&P 500.

Frequently Asked Questions

Should I use my 401(k) to start a business?

ROBS (Rollover as Business Startup): It allows you to use 401k funds tax-free. BUT, it is high risk. If the business fails, you lose your job AND your retirement. Generally avoid.

Can I use a credit card?

Only if you have a 0% APR intro offer AND the cash to pay it off. Using high-interest debt to fund a startup is a death spiral.

What if I can't save that much?

Start the business as a 'Side Hustle' on nights/weekends. Grow it slowly. Only quit when the side hustle income equals 75% of your day job income.
